chunks: Draw a buck converter circuit. The question: Draw a circuit for a buck converter.
Drawing a buck converter means placing a few parts in the right order. A switch connects the input to a middle point called the switch node.
A diode (or second transistor) connects ground to that node. An inductor runs from the node to the output, and a capacitor sits across the load.
Each part has one job in the on-off cycle.
Imagine a heavy truck driving along one road from the switch to the load. The switch is a traffic light on the road from the input.
When the light turns red, the truck cannot stop at once, so it needs a side ramp from ground to keep rolling. That side ramp is the diode.
The capacitor is a small reservoir beside the road that evens out the flow.
Read the schematic left to right.

Q 1 connects V in to the switch node SW; the diode's cathode sits on SW so it is reverse-biased while Q 1 conducts; the inductor carries current left to right in both states; C in sits right at the switch.
Switch node (SW): the junction between the switch, diode and inductor. High-side switch: the transistor between the input and SW.
Freewheel diode: gives the inductor current a path when the switch is off. Inductor: sits in series between SW and the output ("Inductor differential equation").
Synchronous buck: a version where a second transistor replaces the diode.
Draw the input source, then a transistor from its positive side to SW. Draw a diode from ground to SW, with its cathode (bar) at SW.
Draw an inductor from SW to the output node, then a capacitor from the output to ground with the load beside it.
With the switch on, current goes input, switch, inductor, load, ground. With it off, it goes ground, diode, inductor, load. That is the whole idea.
"I'd draw the input source with a capacitor across it, then a high-side NFET from the input rail to a switch node.
From the switch node, a diode down to ground with the cathode at the node, and an inductor going right to the output.
At the output, a capacitor to ground in parallel with the load. A feedback divider goes back to the controller, which drives the FET gate with PWM.
For a synchronous buck I replace the diode with a low-side NFET driven complementary to the top one."
